items.prompt: What job does the visible, cupped part of your outer ear do?

options.label: It filters out background noise before it reaches the eardrum
options.feedback: Filtering happens deeper in the hearing system, not by shape alone.

options.label: It produces sound to help with balance
options.feedback: Nothing in the outer ear generates sound; balance is handled by a completely different structure inside the ear.

options.label: It keeps insects from reaching the eardrum
options.feedback: It does keep some things out, but that is a side effect of its shape, not the reason for the shape.

options.label: It collects and funnels sound waves inward
options.feedback: Its folds and ridges catch sound arriving from many directions and channel it inward.

items.ok_line: The visible shape of the ear is doing real work before any sound reaches the eardrum.
items.ko_title: Not a filter, and not for looks
items.ko_line: The shape isn't sorting sound or making it — it's gathering it.
items.exp_title: A cupped funnel that catches sound
items.exp_text: The folds and ridges of the outer ear are shaped to catch sound waves coming from many directions and reflect them inward toward the opening of the ear canal. That funnelling shape channels the gathered sound into one narrow opening, instead of letting it scatter past the head unused.

items.prompt: Why is the ear canal a narrow tube rather than a wide open space?

options.label: A narrow tube boosts certain sound frequencies on the way to the eardrum
options.feedback: A tube of that particular length naturally reinforces sound waves that fit it.

options.label: It keeps the eardrum from ever getting wet
options.feedback: The canal does help keep the eardrum drier than open skin would, but that is not why it is shaped like a tube.

options.label: It slows sound down so the eardrum has time to react
options.feedback: Sound moves through air at the same pace whether the space is wide or narrow; the tube shape does not change that.

options.label: It stops sound from reaching the eardrum too directly
options.feedback: The tube does the opposite — it channels sound straight at the eardrum rather than blocking the approach.

items.ok_title: A tube tuned like a pipe
items.ok_line: The shape of the canal isn't incidental — it's doing the same thing as blowing across a bottle.
items.ko_line: Sound travels at the same speed through any width of air; the narrowness is doing something else entirely.
items.exp_title: A tube tuned like a tiny organ pipe
items.exp_text: A tube of a certain length and width naturally reinforces sound waves whose length fits it, the same way blowing across a bottle produces one particular note more strongly than others. The ear canal is shaped and sized so that this natural reinforcement lines up with the frequencies carried by human speech, boosting them before the sound wave ever reaches the eardrum.

items.prompt: What does the eardrum actually do when a sound wave reaches it?

options.label: It filters out unwanted frequencies
options.feedback: Sorting frequencies happens much deeper in the ear, inside the cochlea.

options.label: It vibrates back and forth in step with the air pressure changes
options.feedback: It is a thin, stretched membrane, free to move with the rising and falling pressure of the sound wave.

options.label: It absorbs the sound so it doesn't travel further
options.feedback: If the eardrum simply absorbed sound and stopped it there, nothing further inside the ear would ever move.

options.label: It amplifies the sound before passing it on
options.feedback: Amplifying happens after the eardrum, through the small bones behind it; the drum itself just follows the pressure changes.

items.ok_line: The eardrum doesn't judge the sound — it just copies its shape in movement.
items.ko_title: It doesn't stop the sound, and it doesn't sort it
items.ko_line: Whatever the eardrum does, something further along the chain clearly still receives the sound — so what is the drum's own, simple job?
items.exp_title: A membrane that copies the air's motion
items.exp_text: A sound wave is really a rapid back-and-forth pattern of higher and lower air pressure, and the eardrum is a thin, tightly stretched membrane free to move with exactly that pattern. It flexes inward when pressure rises and springs back out when pressure falls, tracing the shape of the sound wave in its own motion.

items.prompt: Why does the ear need three tiny bones between the eardrum and the inner ear?

options.label: To store sound briefly before sending it onward
options.feedback: Nothing in the middle ear holds a vibration in place; each bone passes the motion on almost the instant it receives it.

options.label: To convert vibration into a chemical signal
options.feedback: Turning vibration into a nerve signal happens later, inside the cochlea; the bones only pass mechanical motion along.

options.label: To boost the force of the vibration before it reaches the fluid inside
options.feedback: The three linked bones act as a small lever, concentrating force onto a smaller area.

options.label: To slow the vibration down to a safer speed
options.feedback: The bones don't change how fast the vibration is; they change how much force it carries.

items.ok_title: A lever built for force, not speed
items.ok_line: Three small bones exist to push harder, not to slow anything down.
items.ko_line: The bones are still mechanical, still moving — think about what changes between one end of the chain and the other.
items.exp_title: A lever built to push harder, not faster
items.exp_text: The fluid inside the inner ear is far harder to set moving than air is, so a vibration that easily shakes the eardrum would barely stir that fluid if passed on unchanged. The three linked bones act as a small lever and a size mismatch between two membranes, concentrating the same amount of force onto a smaller area so it arrives strong enough to move the liquid beyond.

items.prompt: Why does the vibration have to cross from air to liquid inside the ear at all?

options.label: Because liquid carries sound more clearly over long distances
options.feedback: The inner ear isn't about carrying sound far — the whole path from eardrum to cochlea is only a short distance inside the skull.

options.label: Because air would evaporate inside the skull
options.feedback: The middle ear already contains air, sealed and undisturbed, with nothing there at risk of evaporating.

options.label: Because liquid vibrates more slowly, giving the ear time to process
options.feedback: The fluid moves in step with the vibration, not slower than it.

options.label: Because the nerve cells that detect sound sit in fluid, not air
options.feedback: The hair cells that detect sound need liquid moving past their bristles to bend them.

items.ok_line: The whole ear is built around getting a vibration to the one place that can actually sense it.
items.ko_title: Not distance, not evaporation, not timing
items.ko_line: Something at the very end of the chain needs liquid specifically — work backward from there.
items.exp_title: The final receptors need a liquid to bend in
items.exp_text: The hair cells that actually detect sound are packed inside a fluid-filled chamber, because their fine bristles need liquid moving past them to bend and trigger a signal. Air arriving at the oval window has to hand its motion over to that internal fluid, which is why the middle ear exists at all — to carry the vibration across from an airborne form into a waterborne one.

items.prompt: How does a moving fluid inside the cochlea end up as a nerve signal?

options.label: The fluid itself carries an electrical charge
options.feedback: The fluid moving is a mechanical event; it only creates the motion that leads to a signal.

options.label: Pressure builds up until a valve releases a signal
options.feedback: There's no valve or pressure threshold here — the process is continuous bending, not a release.

options.label: Tiny hair-like bristles on special cells get bent by the moving fluid
options.feedback: That bending opens channels in the cell and triggers an electrical signal.

options.label: Sound waves shake the nerve fibres directly
options.feedback: The nerve fibres themselves don't respond to sound; they only pick up what the hair cells pass along to them.

items.ok_title: A bend that opens a gate
items.ok_line: The final step from motion to signal happens inside one specific kind of cell.
items.ko_title: No charge in the fluid, no valve
items.ko_line: Something has to physically move to trigger the signal — what's standing in the fluid's path?
items.exp_title: Bending bristles that switch cells on
items.exp_text: Rows of specialised cells inside the cochlea carry tiny stiff bristles on their tops, standing in the path of the moving fluid. When the fluid washes past and tips those bristles over, it pulls open channels in the cell and triggers a burst of electrical activity that travels onward along the nerve.

items.prompt: How does the ear tell a high-pitched sound from a low-pitched one?

options.label: Fast sounds heat the fluid, slow ones don't
options.feedback: Sound doesn't meaningfully heat the fluid at all; pitch has nothing to do with temperature.

options.label: Different pitches make different hair cells fire on their own timer
options.feedback: Hair cells don't run on independent timers; which ones fire depends on where the vibration peaks along the coiled tube.

options.label: Different frequencies peak at different points along the coiled tube
options.feedback: The tube grows wider and floppier along its length, so different points respond to different frequencies.

options.label: High and low sounds arrive through two separate ear canals
options.feedback: Every sound, whatever its pitch, travels in through the same single canal and the same eardrum.

items.ok_line: Pitch is read from where along the tube the vibration peaks, not from any internal clock.
items.ko_title: Not heat, not timers, not separate paths
items.ko_line: Every sound shares the same canal and the same eardrum — the sorting happens later, and it happens by position.
items.exp_title: A coiled tube sorted by frequency
items.exp_text: The tube inside the cochlea is not uniform along its length — it grows wider and its lining grows floppier as it coils inward, so different points along it respond best to different frequencies. A fast vibration sets up its peak ripple near the stiff, narrow start of the tube, while a slow one peaks further along, near the wide, floppy end, so which hair cells respond depends on the pitch of the sound.

items.prompt: What tells the ear how loud a sound is, as opposed to what pitch it is?

options.label: How far the hair-cell bristles get bent
options.feedback: A harder push from the fluid tips the bristles further over, changing how strongly the cell responds.

options.label: Which ear the sound reaches first
options.feedback: That comparison is used to work out where a sound is coming from, not how loud it is.

options.label: How long the sound lasts
options.feedback: A sound can be brief and loud, or long and quiet; duration and loudness are independent of each other.

options.label: How many different pitches are mixed together
options.feedback: A sound made of many mixed pitches isn't automatically louder than a pure, single tone.

items.ok_title: Loudness is about how far, not how long
items.ok_line: The same bristles that sort pitch by position also report loudness by how far they tip.
items.ko_title: Not timing, not duration, not mixture
items.ko_line: Loudness and pitch are read from the same bristles, but by two different properties of their bending.
items.exp_title: A bigger push makes a bigger bend
items.exp_text: A louder sound carries more energy in its air-pressure swings, so it pushes the cochlear fluid with more force. The fluid's push tips the hair-cell bristles over by an amount that matches the force behind it, and that tipping — not any change in pitch — is what the nervous system reads as loudness.

items.prompt: Why do your ears sometimes feel blocked and then suddenly 'pop' when a plane takes off or lands?

options.label: The eardrum temporarily stops vibrating
options.feedback: The eardrum keeps vibrating with sound the whole time; the blocked feeling comes from pressure, not from the drum switching off.

options.label: A narrow tube briefly opens to equalise air pressure behind the eardrum
options.feedback: A passage to the back of the throat normally stays closed, and opens briefly to let trapped air escape or in.

options.label: Fluid drains out of the inner ear
options.feedback: Nothing is draining from the fluid-filled inner ear during a pressure change; the space involved is on the air-filled side of the eardrum.

options.label: The ossicles lock together under pressure
options.feedback: The tiny bones keep moving freely throughout; they don't seize up in response to altitude.

items.ok_line: The pop is a passage catching up on equalising pressure that changed faster outside than in.
items.ko_title: Not the drum, not the fluid, not the bones
items.ko_line: Something on the air-filled side of the eardrum has fallen out of balance with the air outside.
items.exp_title: A pressure valve to the back of the throat
items.exp_text: A narrow passage connects the air-filled space behind the eardrum to the back of the throat, and it normally stays closed, sealing that space off. As outside air pressure changes faster than the trapped air behind the eardrum can match, the drum gets pushed out of its resting position and sound feels muffled — until swallowing or yawning briefly opens the passage and lets the trapped air rush through to match the pressure outside.

items.prompt: How can you tell which direction a sound came from, using two ears instead of one?

options.label: One ear is simply built to detect direction and the other detects volume
options.feedback: Both ears do the same job as each other; direction comes from comparing the two.

options.label: The sound arrives at the two ears at very slightly different moments and volumes
options.feedback: Whichever ear is nearer the sound gets it first and slightly louder, and the two are compared.

options.label: Only the left ear can detect where sound is coming from
options.feedback: Both ears contribute equally to the comparison; neither one works alone for this.

options.label: The head blocks sound completely from one side
options.feedback: The head softens sound reaching the far ear, but it does not block it off entirely.

items.ok_line: Direction comes from the gap between the two ears' reports, not from either ear alone.
items.ko_line: Both ears do the exact same job; whatever tells direction comes from comparing them.
items.exp_title: Two ears compared against each other
items.exp_text: Unless a sound comes from directly ahead or behind, it has a shorter path to whichever ear is nearer, so it arrives there first and slightly louder, since the head itself softens the sound reaching the farther ear. The nervous system compares those tiny differences in timing and loudness between the two ears and uses the pattern to work out the direction the sound came from.
